plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Literacy, Years 5 and 6: creating a persuasive text independently for a named audience, assessed by the Term 4 writing CAT
plan.shape: assessment day: a short review, the CAT explained, one check of what a ready plan looks like, then 40 minutes of protected independent writing
plan.criticalFeature: a contention that answers the persuasive question, held up by three different reasons
decisionPoints: the question check: is the chosen question copied at the top of Elastik page 1?
the plan check: which plan is ready to write?
the 10-minute thumbs check on the plan slide: is the plan finished? (self-report only)
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Introduction claims, body paragraphs prove, conclusion sells.
plan.catchUp: Away for Week 4? Give them the placemat to look at and start them on the plan slide with everyone else; the plan and the placemat walk them through every part.

studentTools: Elastik lined pages, 3 per student, printed from Elastik before the session (names print automatically)
Writer's notebooks, and a Plan Template on every desk (using it is optional)
Class copies of The Last Bear, for ideas only
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: The plan slide, then the writing placemat, on the TV for the whole writing time
Write the finish time on the board: plan done by 10 minutes in
Staff rubric to hand for marking on Elastik after Session 2

slides.notes: Open the session: today and tomorrow every student writes their persuasive CAT, on their own.

Put a Plan Template on every desk. Print the Elastik pages: open the task in Elastik, More, Print, Print template. Number of pages: 3. Template: A4 Straight Lines (8mm). Have writer's notebooks, pencils and The Last Bear out.

slides.title: For the teacher: the CAT week
lines: Wednesday and Thursday: students write the persuasive CAT on their own, on lined pages printed from Elastik. There is no CAT booklet.
To print: open the task in Elastik, then More, Print, Print template. Number of pages: 3. Template: A4 Straight Lines (8mm). Names print automatically.
You mark ONLY the Elastik pages handed in at the end of Thursday. Plans are not collected or marked, and neither is Friday's published copy.
No enabling support while the CAT runs: no content conferencing, no supported sheets. Only learning plan adjustments apply; only absent students get catch-up.
Teaching is about 17 minutes on Wednesday, less on Thursday. Protect the 40 minutes of writing: voices off, plan then placemat on the TV, timings in their notes.
Week 4 taught two reasons plus an answer back. The CAT asks for three body paragraphs; students are told the other side goes inside one of them.
slides.notes: Read before the week. Plans go in writer's notebooks or on the Plan Template. Upload Thursday afternoon. Hand back each student's pages once theirs show as uploaded; an absentee's stay with you until their catch-up is uploaded.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to show everything we know about persuasive writing in one piece we write on our own.
successCriteria: I can choose a topic and plan my contention and three reasons.
I can write an introduction and body paragraphs that claim it and prove it.
I can choose words and tricks that persuade my reader.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: For the next two days, you get to show us
everything you can do as a persuasive writer.
SAY: Let's read the I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Choosing and planning is where everyone starts.
Then the writing itself is today's big goal.
notes.prep: SC1 is the plan (writer's notebook or Plan Template), SC2 the writing on the Elastik pages, SC3 the persuasive language. Keep it brisk: 1 minute.

slides.title: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.
slides.prompt: Which part of your writing does each job?

notes.answer: introduction claims, body paragraphs prove, conclusion sells
beats: SAY: These three pictures carried us through every piece last week.
Today they carry your CAT.
ASK: Which part of your writing claims it, which proves it, and which sells it?
15 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 15 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: introduction claims, body proves, conclusion sells
SAY: That's it. Let's warm up with three quick sentences.
You'll tell me which job each one does.
trap: putting the call to action in the introduction.
Fix: ask what the last thing your reader should hear is. Student moves it.
notes.prep: Re-grounds the Week 4 structure for everyone, including anyone who was away. 2 minutes.

slides.title: Claim it, prove it or sell it?
slides.pivot: ask which job it does: claim, prove or sell
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which words told you?

visual.text: Most importantly, a bike shed keeps bikes dry, so more kids ride to school.

items.label: 1 Claim it | 2 Prove it | 3 Sell it
items.pivot: ask which words show a reason: Most importantly
items.say: Two, prove it. Most importantly tells us it's a reason. Tick it or fix it.

visual.text: So please sign our petition for a bike shed before the end of term.

items.label: 1 Claim it | 2 Prove it | 3 Sell it
items.pivot: ask does it tell the reader to do something?
items.say: Three, sell it. It asks the reader to act. Tick it or fix it.

visual.text: Have you ever ridden to school and sat on a soaking wet seat?

items.label: 1 Claim it | 2 Prove it | 3 Sell it
items.answer: 1 - claim it (a hook in the introduction)
items.pivot: ask is it a question to grab me at the start?
items.say: One, claim it. It's a hook to grab the reader. Tick it or fix it.

say: Show me 1 for claim it, 2 for prove it, 3 for sell it.
These sentences are about a bike shed, not your CAT topics.
trap: choosing by the topic words, not the job the sentence does.
Fix: ask what job it does for the reader. Student re-shows.
notes.stretch: Which words in the sentence told you its job?
notes.help: Point to the placemat panels while they decide.
notes.prep: Brisk retrieval of the three jobs before the task. Off-topic on purpose so nothing can be copied into the CAT. 2 minutes.

slides.ask: Which job does this sentence do?

slides.meaning: Your position: what you want your reader to agree with.
slides.example: I believe every school should have a bike shed.

notes.answer: your position: what you want the reader to agree with
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: The CAT uses this word. Say it with me.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Contention is just another word for your position.
It's the one sentence that tells your reader which side you're on.
ASK: Does the example answer a yes or no question with a side?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
trap: writing the topic, like Climate change, instead of a side.
Fix: ask what do you believe should happen? Student rewrites it as I believe...
notes.prep: The CAT plan says position / contention. One word card so nobody stalls on it. 1 minute.

rows: One persuasive text about an environmental or animal issue
Students in Grades 5 and 6 at other local primary schools
On your own, on lined Elastik pages
Today and tomorrow, then you publish on Friday
Something a Grade 5 or 6 student can do

notes.answer: Grade 5 and 6 students at other schools; banning plastic bags: thumbs down
beats: POINT to What. SAY: This is the real thing, written on your own.
POINT to Who reads it.
SAY: Not me or the principal: kids your age at other schools.
ASK: Who are you writing to convince?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Grade 5 and 6 students
POINT to Call to action.
SAY: Make it something a Grade 5 or 6 student can do.
ASK: Can a Grade 5 or 6 student do this? Ban plastic bags in Australia.
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs down
trap: a call to action aimed at governments or adults (watch topics 1 and 3).
Fix: ask what a Grade 5 or 6 student could do. e.g. Join a green team.
notes.prep: The CAT task, read aloud. Audience is a rubric row; a call to action aimed only at adults sits below 5.0 (staff rubric calibration). 3 minutes.

slides.title: Step 1: four topics to choose from

visual.banner: The CAT's own ideas: you don't need them all

panels.heading: 4 School
lines: Last Bear: one person can help

beats: SAY: Here are the four CAT topics, with the CAT's own ideas.
You don't need them all.
SAY: Look for the topic you can prove three ways.
You can use The Last Bear and what you know.
ASK: Which topic are you leaning towards right now?
15 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, voices off... show me.
EXPECT: 1, 2, 3 or 4
trap: choosing a topic because a friend did.
Fix: ask can you name three reasons now? If not, they look again.
notes.prep: The CAT's own Ideas to get you started and Last Bear links, the same for every class. Fingers give a quick read of the topic spread. 2 minutes.

rows: Should governments and communities do more to protect animals from the effects of climate change?
Should protecting natural habitats be more important than clearing land for human development?
Should humans do more to protect endangered animals, even when conservation is expensive or difficult?
Should every school be required to have an environmental action plan?

notes.answer: thumbs up: the question copied at the top of Elastik page 1
beats: HAND OUT the Elastik pages.
SAY: Choose your question now.
SAY: Copy it at the top of Elastik page 1, word for word.
Keep this slide up while they copy.
ASK: Is your question copied at the top of page 1?
10 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
SCAN for thumbs down.
80%+ -> move on.
Less -> SAY: Copy the line that ends with a question mark. Re-ask.
trap: copying the topic name, not the question.
Fix: student copies the line that ends with a question mark.
notes.prep: Questions copied exactly from the CAT. The question on page 1 lets markers judge whether the contention answers it. 2 minutes.

slides.title: Which plan is ready to write?
slides.prompt: Question: Should every school have a bike shed?

options.text: Bikes are great because they are fun, fast and healthy.
options.misconception: writes about the topic instead of answering the question with a side

options.text: Every school needs a bike shed: it keeps bikes dry, stops theft and gets more kids riding.
Every school needs a bike shed because rain wets bikes, soaks seats and rusts chains.
options.misconception: gives one reason three ways, not three different reasons

notes.answer: B - it takes a side and has three different reasons
beats: SAY: Before you plan, let's check what a ready plan looks like.
Read all three in your head.
ASK: Which plan is ready to write?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> cold call one B: Why not C? Then reveal.
Less -> cover the words, count C's reasons aloud: all rain. Re-ask.
trap: choosing C because it has three parts.
Fix: student names each reason in two words and spots that all three are rain.
notes.prep: The decision point before release. Three different reasons is what the CAT's three body paragraphs need.

slides.title: Your turn: choose, plan, write
slides.task: Work on your own. Plan first, then write on your Elastik pages.
steps: Plan your contention, hook and three reasons.
Write your introduction on your Elastik pages.
Write your body paragraphs, one reason each.
slides.where: Writer's notebook or Plan Template, then Elastik pages
slides.visualLabel: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.
slides.extendedTask: the persuasive CAT: plan, then write the introduction and body paragraphs on the Elastik pages

notes.answer: a plan, an introduction and at least one body paragraph
beats: SAY: Let's read the steps together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Last week you wrote two reasons and an answer back.
The CAT needs three different reasons, one in each body paragraph.
Your answer back now sits inside one of them, with a reason.
ASK: How many body paragraphs does your CAT need?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, voices off... show me.
EXPECT: 3
SAY: Plan in your notebook or on the template, your choice.
Voices off now, all your own work. SHOW the plan slide.
trap: planning two reasons and an answer back.
Fix: student adds a third different reason to their plan.
notes.stretch: Finished early? Reread your piece against every line of the placemat.
notes.help: Learning plan adjustments only. Point to the placemat panel they need.
notes.prep: Independent writing. Give no ideas, sentences or spelling during the CAT. SC1 and SC2.

rows: At the top of Elastik page 1. Your contention answers it.
My contention: what I want readers to agree with
A question, a surprising fact, Imagine..., a mini-story or a bold statement

notes.answer: thumbs up at 10 minutes: plan finished
beats: SHOW this slide for the first 10 minutes. CIRCULATE, but give no ideas.
If asked, SAY: Check the plan on the board.
ASK: At 10 minutes: Is your plan finished?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
SCAN the thumbs only. Do not check or comment on plans.
80%+ -> SAY: Plan done? Start your introduction.
Less -> SAY to everyone: Three different reasons, then start writing. Re-ask at 15.
SWITCH to the placemat at 10 minutes, or at 15 if you re-asked.
notes.prep: The CAT's own plan prompts, the same in every class. Plans go in writer's notebooks or the Plan Template and are not collected or marked.

visual.banner: Your reader: Grade 5 and 6 students at other local primary schools

lines: This means... why it matters to your reader
In one body paragraph, answer the other side: Some people might think... However, I believe... because...

beats: SHOW this slide from the plan check to the end.
CIRCULATE, but give no ideas or sentences.
If asked, SAY: Check your plan and the placemat.

notes.answer: open - an underlined contention that takes a side on the question
beats: SAY: Pencils down. Let's read our I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
ASK: Underline your contention. Does it answer your question?
30 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
RECORD each thumb down. Tomorrow, they reread their plan first.

organiser.right: Persuasive question, and ideas to get you started
rightContent: Should governments and communities do more to protect animals from the effects of climate change? Ideas: changing habitats, reducing pollution, protecting wildlife for the future. The Last Bear: Bear's changing Arctic.

Should protecting natural habitats be more important than clearing land for human development? Ideas: safe places for animals to live, the risk of extinction, sharing the planet with wildlife. The Last Bear: Bear's isolation.

Should humans do more to protect endangered animals, even when conservation is expensive or difficult? Ideas: healthy ecosystems, conservation programs, protecting wildlife for future generations. The Last Bear: April and Bear.

Should every school be required to have an environmental action plan? Ideas: reducing waste, saving water and energy, how small actions make a difference. The Last Bear: one person can make a difference.
